'''Robert Graham Hamish Robertson''' (born 3 October 1943) is a [[Canadian Americans|Canadian–American]] [[Experimental physics|experimental physicist]], specializing in [[neutrino]] physics.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Haxton|first1=W.C.|author1link= Wick Haxton|last2=Hamish Robertson|first2=R.G. |last3=Serenelli|first3=Aldo M.|title=Solar Neutrinos: Status and Prospects|journal=[[Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics]]|date=18 August 2013|volume=51|issue=1|pages=21–61|doi=10.1146/annurev-astro-081811-125539|arxiv = 1208.5723 |bibcode = 2013ARA&A..51...21H }}</ref> He is a [[Professor emeritus|Professor Emeritus]] at the [[University of Washington]], where he was formerly the director of the University of Washington's Center for Experimental Nuclear Physics and Astrophysics.

==Biography==
Robertson was born in Ottawa, Canada, in 1943 and attended elementary and secondary school in Canada and England.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Zierler |first=David |date=2021-09-24 |title=Hamish Robertson |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44411 |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=www.aip.org |language=en}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[University of Oxford]] in 1965. In 1971, he received a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] from [[McMaster University]], working under R. G. Summers-Gill with a dissertation titled ''Properties of the odd-odd cobalt nuclei''.

== Career ==

=== Michigan State University ===
After completing his Ph.D., Robertson joined [[Michigan State University]] as a postdoctoral fellow and later became a faculty member, earning the rank of Professor of Physics in 1981.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics Recipient |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Robertson&first_nm=Hamish&year=1997 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181027021705/https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Robertson&first_nm=Hamish&year=1997 |archive-date=2018-10-27 |access-date=2017-12-24 |website=[[American Physical Society]] |language=en}}</ref> During his tenure, he conducted pioneering experiments in [[nuclear astrophysics]], including resolving the origins of [[Isotopes of lithium|lithium-6]] through sensitive deuterium-helium-4 capture measurements.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Overgaard |first=Elise |date=2023-01-24 |title=Ways to weigh a neutrino {{!}} symmetry magazine |url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/ways-to-weigh-a-neutrino?language_content_entity=und |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=www.symmetrymagazine.org |language=en}}</ref> He also contributed to parity violation and nuclear reaction studies, and his research identified the first isobaric quintet of states in nuclei.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hamish Robertson {{!}} Sanford Underground Research Facility |url=https://sanfordlab.org/people/hamish-robertson |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=sanfordlab.org |language=en}}</ref>

In 1976, Robertson was awarded an [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Alfred P. Sloan Foundation Fellowship]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Los Alamos National Laboratory ===
In 1981, Robertson joined the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] (LANL), where his research shifted toward [[Neutrino|neutrino physics]].<ref name="RGHRpage">{{cite web |title=Hamish Robertson's Web Page |url=http://faculty.washington.edu/rghr/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181008051829/http://faculty.washington.edu/rghr/ |archive-date=2018-10-08 |access-date=2016-04-15 |website=faculty.washington.edu |postscript=; contains selected publications with ArXiv.org links}}</ref>  His work on tritium beta decay provided constraints on the electron neutrino mass, showing it was insufficient to close the universe gravitationally. Robertson also spearheaded LANL's collaboration in the [[Sudbury Neutrino Observatory]] (SNO), an experiment that confirmed neutrino flavor oscillations, challenging the Standard Model of particle physics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=R. G. Hamish Robertson – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/r-g-hamish-robertson-nd1mcl/ |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=NasOnLINE |language=en-US}}</ref>

In recognition of his contributions, he was appointed as a Fellow of Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1988.<ref name=":0" />

=== University of Washington ===
In 1994, he became a [[professor]] at the [[University of Washington]]. He continued his research on neutrino physics, including work with the [[KATRIN]] Experiment and Project 8, which aimed to measure the [[Neutrino|neutrino mass]] with unprecedented sensitivity. <ref>{{Cite web |last=Urton |first=James |last2=Washington |first2=University of |title=KATRIN cuts the mass estimate for the elusive neutrino in half |url=https://phys.org/news/2019-09-results-mass-neutrinos.html |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=phys.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Colloquium - Hamish Robertson (University of Washington) - Progress Toward Measuring the Mass of the Neutrino {{!}} Department of Physics |url=https://physics.osu.edu/events/colloquium-hamish-robertson-university-washington-progress-toward-measuring-mass-neurtrino |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=physics.osu.edu |language=en}}</ref>He was named to the Boeing Distinguished Professorship in 2008 and retired as Professor Emeritus in 2017.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/10583/chapter/10#75 |title=Read "Neutrinos and Beyond: New Windows on Nature" at NAP.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Robertson has been a visiting scientist at several institutions, including at [[Princeton University]] (1975–1976), [[Chalk River Laboratories]] (1979), [[Argonne National Laboratory]] (1980), and the [[Sudbury Neutrino Observatory]] (2003–2004).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?robertsonrgh |title=R. G. Robertson {{!}} Array of Contemporary American Physicists |access-date=2016-04-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160508084552/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?robertsonrgh |archive-date=2016-05-08 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was on the editorial staff of ''[[Physical Review D]]'' and the ''[[Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science]]''.

==Awards and honours==
* 1976: Awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Sloan Foundation Fellowship]]
* 1982: Elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]
* 1997: [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]], American Physical Society
* 1998: Elected a Fellow of the [[Institute of Physics]] (London)
* 2003: Elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
* 2004: Elected a Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]]
